speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Judicial review by the Supreme Court represents an important tenet of the Rule of Law that all power must have legal limits.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In our Westminster-styled Government, Executive action is generally reviewable by the Judiciary, which is vested with judicial power under Article 93 of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Article 4 of the Constitution states that any law enacted by this House which is inconsistent with the Constitution shall be void.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Judicial review does not mean that the Court substitutes its decision for the Executive's decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What it means is that the Court has a right to satisfy itself of the legality, rationality, and procedural propriety of the Executive's decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If it is not satisfied, it can strike such action down as being of no effect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In comparison, Parliament, to which the Executive is accountable to, does not have such a power, although it has other tools.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, structurally, the Executive is drawn from the majority of elected Members of Parliament in Parliament; a feature that Walter Bagehot referred to as the "efficient secret of the English Constitution" upon which the Westminster-styled Government is based on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Singapore, most Government actions are subject to judicial review.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is noteworthy that even where public safety and peace are at threat, is recognised that the Minister's decisions based on such matters may be judicially reviewed by the Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I would refer to these clauses as ouster clauses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The big elephant in the room, of course, the Internal Security Act or the ISA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the impact of such provisions on the Rule of Law, I think it is desirable that this House regularly conduct a review of the ouster clauses against current circumstances to ensure that there continues to be a need for such exceptions to exist and strike an appropriate balance between efficiency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, it is important for each generation of political leaders and people to find their own equilibrium of what our people would accept without question, under what circumstances and towards what ends.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Fellow Singaporeans' desires and expectations are by no means static.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our Prime Minister, in his speech as Secretary-General of the PAP at its 36th Ordinary Party Conference in November 2020, acknowledged this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He stated that Singaporeans today have expressed a desire to, amongst others, re-examine basic assumptions, look beyond, tried and tested ways of doing things and have greater checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He also said that the PAP Government must change and respond to these desires and expectations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Law derives its power not merely from the fact that it is enforceable by the state apparatus, but, fundamentally, from our people's willingness to accept the law and the authority of our institutions as legitimate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, our people trust all three pillars of our Government to enact, use and enforce laws to ensure that we remain a fair and just, safe and secure society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must not take this trust for granted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As Members of this House, we are the people's representatives and part of the eco-system that ensures our people's acceptance of the legitimacy of laws and institutions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before looking at the statutes in question, I think it is worthwhile mentioning that, thus far, the Government has taken a careful approach to clauses ousting judicial review.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even in relation to the CLTPA, in respect of which, hon Members may recall, the Court of Appeal issued a judgment quashing the Minister's detention order in 2015.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister, when he moved the Bill in this House 2018 to extend the validity of CLTPA for another five years, he made it very clear that his decisions under the Act may continue to be judicially reviewed on the three established grounds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I read this as a deliberate decision on the part of the Government to keep the exceptions to what it considers to be necessary in public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With that, let me move straight to the ISA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to state upfront that I believe that there remains a cogent basis to maintain the status quo for ISA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The ISA is an extraordinary piece of legislation that is aimed at ensuring Singapore's stability and security.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I closely read the debate introducing the ouster clause in the ISA in 1989, particularly the speech of the then Minister of Home Affairs, the hon Prof S Jayakumar.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a bitingly frank response to points made by hon Members of Parliament, he recognised that there could be a prospect of the powers under ISA being misused.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, he stated that ISA deals with issues where national security is involved and putting a Court to scrutinise exercise of powers will be tantamount to giving the Court, an unelected body, the final say on such matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That, in the scheme of things, is not desirable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is not to say that the Minister will be given a carte blanche.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In lieu of Court scrutiny, both the ISA and the Constitution prescribed safeguards, such as the involvement of an Advisory Board and the elected President.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There could also be judicial review on the ground of non-compliance with procedural requirements under the ISA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In short, the ISA does not operate in darkness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are checks and balances that involve, amongst others, the office of the Elected President.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Just a few weeks ago, we saw the Minister for Home Affairs exercise his detention power against a self-radicalised young person professing to be Christian who planned to attack Muslims with a machete at two mosques.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Fellow Singaporeans would have been greatly disturbed by this attempt to sow discord and hatred between religious groups here.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This case demonstrates that the continued relevance of ISA against the context of the ever-growing threat of radicalisation, extremism and terrorism on our shores.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister for Home Affairs reminded us poignantly that these extremists "have to succeed only once, but ISD has to succeed every single time".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Outside the realm of national security, we have statutes that contain ouster clauses excluding judicial review.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Most times, the Parliamentary intention in enacting these ouster clauses is to allow the Executive to move quickly and efficiently and make final and dispositive decisions in national interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The general purpose of the Charities Act is to register charities and regulate the conduct of their fund-raising activities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the Charities Act, the Commissioner has the power to prohibit persons from conducting any fund-raising if he is satisfied that the fund raising should not be conducted, generally, in public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His decision and that of the Minister, in this regard, is not subject to judicial review save in relation to compliance with any procedural requirement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Senior Minister Teo, in his capacity as Minister of State for Finance, explained in 1994 when moving the Bill as follows, and I quote, "Clause 40 will ensure that the merits of the decision cannot be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is to avoid a situation where interested parties can through the Courts frustrate Government's decision to reject an application for a fund-raising permit." Under the Immigration Act, the Government has the power to deal with immigration into and departure from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Exercise of such power, however, is not subject to judicial review.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In justifying this position, the then Minister for Home Affairs, Prof Jayakumar stated in 1993 as follows, and I quote, "The intention of this amendment is that the merits of the immigration decision, that is, whether it is right or wrong, cannot be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is to avoid a situation where the Courts can frustrate Government's decision to expel aliens under the Act or other immigration decisions concerning aliens." Under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, decisions of the Minister and the Controller of Work Passes in relation to the issuance, suspension and revocation of work passes are not subject to judicial review.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Dr Ng Eng Heng, then the Minister for Manpower in 2007, explained its rationale as follows, and I quote, "For consistency, certain provisions that are currently under the Immigration Act are also replicated under this Act, including the exemption of the decisions of the Minister and the Controller of Work Passes in relation to the issuance, suspension and revocation of work passes from judicial review." My concern here does not arise just because judicial review is ousted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recognise that there could be areas outside the realm of national security where it may well be desirable in national interest for the Executive to act quickly and efficiently.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, what is as important is that we need ensure that powers vested by Parliament on the Executive will not be abused.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will be consistent with Singaporeans' desire that there should be more checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also need to explain to Singaporeans why a different approach is mandated when dealing with such matters whereas when it comes to Executive action on important matters, such as public safety, peace and good order under the CLTPA, it may be judicially reviewed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Additionally, from time to time, powers vested with the Executive under statutes that exclude judicial review may be used in an evolving variety of scenarios.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For these employers, MOM has withdrawn work pass privileges.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, the target of the powers are no longer aliens, but in certain situations, it may extend to Singapore-based businesses and companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Personally, I am not convinced with the utility argument that has been advanced in Parliament to justify ouster clauses, that persons subject to the Executive’s order may abuse the Court's process by commencing unmeritorious judicial review action just to frustrate legitimate Government action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would point out that that can happen even now since there can be judicial review on the narrower ground of procedural propriety.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: More importantly, our Court is well-equipped to handle unmeritorious cases that amount to an abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may, amongst others, sanctioning not just the party but the counsel representing the party.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is another reason why I think it is a good time to conduct the review of ouster clauses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is a recent decision of the Supreme Court we in this House should take note of.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2019, a five-judge bench of the Court of Appeal handed down its decision in Nagaenthran.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In that case, the appellant, who was convicted for the capital offence of drug trafficking, sought a judicial review of the Public Prosecutor's decision not to issue a certificate of cooperation to him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This has an impact on whether the appellant would be imposed a death sentence or have that substituted with life imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It was argued on behalf of the Public Prosecutor that the provision in the Misuse of Drugs Act allowing the Public Prosecutor the discretion to decide whether to issue the certificate ousts judicial review.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a unanimous decision, the Court held that the provision which the Public Prosecutor relied on was not an ouster clause.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I accept that the Court in Nagaenthran did not decide on the validity of any ouster clause.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, given the reasoning of the Court, this may be an opportune time for the Government to review its position on ouster clauses in the name of good governance and the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I quote the hon the Chief Justice who stated as follows extrajudicially: "In the final analysis, the robustness of a nation's rule of law framework depends greatly on how the other branches view the Judiciary and whether it in turn is able and willing to act honestly, competently and independently." In conclusion, let me say that I am fully aware of the advantage that comes with ensuring that our Executive move speedily, flexibly and effectively to decide matters in the national interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our experience as a nation shows that such ability on the part of the Executive is vital given our country's well-known vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also appreciate that the rule of law should not be viewed a panacea but is a means to an end which is to help to build a fair and just society, a system that works and a vibrant economy that will enable Singaporeans to realise their dreams.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am not advocating a Western style of rule of law that may not suit our circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My basic concern is to address the desire of Singaporeans for greater checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Ultimately, I believe that ensuring the sunlight of scrutiny on Executive action, be it by the Court or another high office, will strengthen the legitimacy of our laws.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our people will be able to rely on the authoritative findings of these institutions to satisfy themselves of the bona fides or otherwise of Government action and that there are, indeed legal limits placed on the powers vested in the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is how the Government should be held accountable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this is how we ensure a bright future for our country.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: His speech raises questions about the relationship between Parliament, the Judiciary and the Executive, and the respective spheres that they inhabit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, to have strong and effective governance, to get things done.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And finally, ensuring the safety of our people.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These indicators show that we have succeeded in achieving our priorities, and more.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: How do these priorities find expression in the system of government and political structure, that we have?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our constitutional framework defines the responsibilities of each branch of government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Parliament, which passes laws to promote these objectives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Through its power to amend the Constitution, Parliament also decides on the overarching framework for our system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Executive, which administers the laws and formulates policies to secure these objectives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the Judiciary, which applies the law faithfully, when disputes are brought before the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In some other systems, the focus has been to tightly circumscribe and police the Executive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This leads to gridlock and inaction and we do not subscribe to this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such an approach loses sight also of another key principle.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the governance system to work, there must be mutual trust and respect, for each branch's institutional expertise and competence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Power and responsibility must be divided, to empower each branch, not divide.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What are the reasons for our approach, Sir?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our system must ensure that we can act quickly, move decisively to navigate challenges, to seize opportunities and avoid crises.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But when crises cannot be avoided, to deal then with them efficiently and effectively.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Parliament and the Executive handle this, and they must account for the success or failure of their policies through the democratic process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our system should empower them to take effective action rather than to impair their ability to act through gridlock.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Their courts have embroiled themselves in the realm of politics and policy-making – not always with happy results.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have set out one example in the handout.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is a lengthy list, as Members will see from the handout, including nursery admissions, the number of free beds in hospitals, the size of speed-breakers on roads, and many others.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Members will agree with me that for Singapore, it is best if these matters are left for the Executive to determine.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In Australia, the Government there has long been beset by litigation over immigration matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Judicial review has been used by non-citizens to prolong their stay, at the cost of public resources.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Australia’s former Minister for Immigration Philip Ruddock has observed that such politically controversial matters, which involve competing objectives and values, were for Parliament to determine as representatives of the people, and I agree.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In England, former Supreme Court Judge, Lord Sumption, has detected, and I quote, "a noticeable change of judicial mood" in recent decades.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The "special cases", once thought to be beyond the courts’ purview, such as foreign policy, "have one by one yielded to the power of the judges", unquote.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is therefore no surprise that civil servants in the UK are now given a detailed 104-page guide – aptly or, perhaps, sardonically – titled "Judge Over Your Shoulder", or "JOYS" to help them assess legal risks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They have also had two rounds of law reform review on judicial review twice in the course of the last eight years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Lord Sumption himself notes that this state of affairs is a product of political reality in the UK – judges have attempted to fill the gap left by politics, as the latter has lost its prestige.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He makes a similar observation of the United States, and what he refers to as "distortions" in their governance structure that have resulted from political gridlock.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In Singapore, we have not gone down this route.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have been, and must remain careful to operate our system to maintain trust, and to keep a constructive balance between the three branches of Government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The approach taken by our Courts has been instrumental to the success of the Singapore approach.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a delicate but very important balance, that not many other jurisdictions have managed to strike successfully.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This judicial philosophy is best encapsulated in our Chief Justice’s remarks in a 2018 lecture, and I quote, "… in Singapore… we have found that executive power can best be checked when courts eschew politics and secure a relationship of trust and respect between the three branches by recognising and maintaining the legitimate space of each. … First, it means that Courts should not see themselves as antagonists whose role is to obstruct governmental action, but rather as equal partners with the other branches in the common project to promote efficient administration and good and proper governance, which the Judiciary contributes to by upholding the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, it means that the Judiciary should not be diffident about performing its constitutional role when called upon to invalidate unlawful action… The difference is between a paradigm of confrontation and containment informed by mutual distrust and self-preservation and one of partnership and cooperation within a framework of governance and legality.” The principles of administrative law in Singapore give expression to this overarching approach and is based on two fundamental principles flowing from the constitutional separation of powers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, the Executive must act within the law, and it is the role of the courts to say what the law is.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Courts can, in general, review executive action on three grounds: illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Each of these grounds leaves wide latitude to the Executive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, and equally importantly, the Courts recognise that the exercise of executive authority is ultimately the responsibility of the Executive and not the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is the Executive which is vested with executive authority under the Constitution; has an elected mandate, which is accountable to Parliament and at the polls; and has the institutional competence and resources to make judgement calls between the competing considerations that often arise in policy decisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I refer Members back to part 2 of Annex 5, which sets out these key principles, and we agree with the approach that the Courts have taken.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It avoids the quagmires often seen overseas, when judiciaries step into the spheres of other branches of government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It leaves matters that are rightly determined by democratically elected bodies in the hands of these elected representatives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And to paraphrase Mr Ruddock, politically controversial matters, which involve competing objectives and values, should be determined by Parliament.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pillai has referred to clauses which exclude or restrict one or more of the grounds for judicial review.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court has held that such ouster or privative clauses are not per se wrong.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have also taken a principled and calibrated approach to the use of such clauses, and they are proposed only after careful consideration of the policy objective behind each of the proposed clauses; whether alternative legislative tools may be employed to achieve this; and whether the clause may be calibrated to restrict only some of the bases for judicial review.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Thereafter, they are subject to rigorous debate in this House, in Parliament, and passed into law with Parliament’s assent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Through this approach, trust – not just within the branches but vis-à-vis each branch and the population at large – has been nurtured and sustained.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pillai has referred to both the Internal Security Act (ISA) and the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act (CLTPA), which both provide for powers of detention.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such powers, as Mr Pillai has acknowledged, are necessary, to allow for pre-emptive action, to safeguard national security, and because criminal prosecution may not be possible, for example, due to evidential difficulties of admissibility.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In these circumstances, Parliament, in accordance with its legislative power, vested the discretion to exercise powers of detention with the Executive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pillai has also cited various other non-security related legislation containing privative clauses, notwithstanding that these are outside the realm of national security, where speed and efficiency are also critical considerations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For a globalised city-state, thriving on open borders and human resources, immigration and foreign manpower – two areas that Mr Murali cited – are key areas of concern.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They require a careful balancing of sensitive and polycentric considerations, such as foreign relations; transborder crime; economic and manpower planning; and protection of businesses and families.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Immigration and foreign manpower have serious implications for our society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The experience of Australia, on immigration challenges in Court, as explained in the handout at part 1 of Annex 5, illustrates why we take the approach that we do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have already seen xenophobia, social schisms develop in other countries and we are not immune to these pressures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It would not be appropriate to litigate such matters because the Courts do not have institutional capability to know of, to consider and to balance the many considerations and concerns involved.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Resolution of policy judgements by the Courts also lacks the democratic legitimacy of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As the Chief Justice noted in the lecture I mentioned earlier, Courts are not especially well placed to answer such social, economic and political questions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is accountable to Parliament and to the people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We must continue to foster a system of governance which maintains a clear eye on outcomes – to improve our citizens’ lives – I refer Members again to the handout on Singapore’s social and economic indicators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is proof of what we have achieved for Singapore with our political and governance system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It demonstrates that our political and judicial system promotes good governance and the rule of law, with clear and tangibly positive outcomes for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have a few minutes left, any clarifications, Mr Pillai?
